documentNotes.title: General Instructions for Theoretical Examination
documentNotes.statement:
Before the Exam

1. The allocated time for theoretical examination is 5 hours for answering 3 questions that carry 10 points each.
2. Please ensure that your student code matches the one on your desk. Place your ID / tag on the top right corner of the desk.
3. Kindly ensure that you have the following items on the desk:
   (i) A sealed envelope containing the Question Papers and Answer Scripts.
   (ii) A labelled envelope.
   (iii) Pens/relevant stationery (You need to bring in your own calculator).
   If you find that the items are incomplete, kindly raise your hands.
4. You must not open the sealed envelopes before the start of the examination.

During the Exam

1. You must use the dedicated answer scripts provided for writing your answers. Write your answers only in boxed answer scripts. If you need more boxed answer scripts, please raise your hand and ask an invigilator. Clearly write your student code and write which question you are attempting on each of your extra requested answer scripts.
2. **There are additional blank draft papers. These will not be marked.**
3. Try to be as concise as possible in your answers: use equations, logical operators, and sketches to illustrate your thoughts whenever possible. Avoid the use of long sentences.
4. Use an appropriate number of significant figures when stating numbers.
5. You are not allowed to leave your working place without permission. If you need any assistance (malfunctioning calculator, need to visit a restroom, insufficient Draft Papers, etc), please draw the attention of the invigilator by raising your hand.

At the end of the Exam

1. At the end of the examination, you must stop writing immediately.
2. Put all the Answer Scripts into the labelled envelope and seal it, including any blank Answer Scripts. It is your responsibility to ensure all Answer Scripts are inside the envelope and submitted to the invigilator.
3. Put question papers and draft papers into another envelope. You are not allowed to take any sheets of paper out of the examination hall.
4. Wait at your table in silence till your envelopes are collected. Once all envelopes are collected, your guide will escort you out of the examination area.

problems.title: Geometry of Water Fountain
problems.statement:
**Introduction**

Water sprayers are found at various places such as agriculture farms, green parks or urban areas for functional purposes or for aesthetic art installation. Consider a hemispherical shaped fountain sprayer of radius $r$ at the height $h$ from the ground as shown in a cross-sectional diagram in **Fig. 1**. Let the radius of the hemisphere to be small compared to the range $R$, hence can be treated as a point source. However there are $\rho(\theta)$ number of holes per unit area at angle $\theta$. The water spurts in all directions at the same initial velocity $v_o$.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Schematic cross section of a hemispherical shaped fountain sprayer.
figures.alt: Cross section of a hemispherical fountain of radius r on a vertical post of height h above the x axis, origin (0,0) at the foot of the post; blue parabolic water trajectories leave the hemisphere at angle θ, one landing at horizontal distance R; labelled boxes read 'hemispherical fountain, radius r with ρ(θ) number of holes per unit area, at angle θ' and 'water projectile trajectory'; axes x and y.

sections.title: Part A: Uniformly Distributed Holes on the Surface of the Hemisphere
sections.statement: First consider the holes distribution on the surface of the hemisphere to be uniform (i.e. $\rho(\theta)$ is a constant).

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement: Express the instantaneous position $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ of a water element (can be treated as a stream of particles) launched at velocity $v_o$ at angle $\theta$.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement: Derive the water trajectory relation $y = y(x, \theta)$ and express in a same type of trigonometric function (e.g. in terms of sine, cosine or tangent ONLY). Note that $\theta > 0$.

parts.label: A.3
parts.statement: The envelope is the minimal boundary which encloses all water trajectories (i.e. no water will be found beyond this boundary). Derive the equation for the envelope for this system. Express your answer as y(x). Sketch the envelope over the trajectories.

parts.label: A.4
parts.statement: Calculate the range $R = R(\theta)$ as a function of angle $\theta$.

parts.label: A.5
parts.statement: Letting $h \to 0$ in the range obtained in **A.4**, show that $R = \frac{v_o^2}{g} \sin 2\theta$.

sections.title: Part B: Non-Uniformly Distributed Holes on the Surface of the Hemisphere
sections.statement: Now, consider the area of holes per unit area $\rho(\theta)$ to be non-uniformly distributed and depended on the angle $\theta$.

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement: Using the results from part **A.4** above, calculate the elemental area $dA_W$ of an annulus (ring) of radius $R$ and width $dR$ of the water hitting the ground. Express your answer in R, R' and d$\theta$. [hint: consider R'=$\frac{dR}{d\theta}$ ]

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement: Determine the relation for $\rho(\theta)$ that gives a uniform spray coverage pattern on the ground by considering elemental area on the hemisphere in proportional to the elemental area of the water spray on the ground. Express your answer in terms of R and its derivative. [hint: consider condition where $R'(\theta) > 0$].

parts.label: B.3
parts.statement: Letting $h = 0$, calculate explicitly the relation for $\rho(\theta)$ that gives a uniform spray coverage pattern for $\theta < 45^{\circ}$.

figures.caption: Sketch of the envelop of water trajectory
figures.alt: Sketch: a hemispherical fountain on a vertical post of height h above the x axis, origin (0,0) at the foot of the post; blue parabolic water trajectories leave the hemisphere at various angles θ and land on the ground, one at horizontal distance R; a thick black parabola touching all trajectories from above is marked with an arrow and the label y = h + v_o²/2g − gx²/2v_o²; axes x and y.

sections.title: Part A: Uniformly Distributed Holes on the Surface of the Hemisphere

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement:
Given the radius of the hemisphere is small compared to the range, that we can treat all the different water sprouts emanate from a point source at the center of the hemisphere at the same initial velocity but at different angles $\theta$. Note that the distribution of the holes on the surface of the hemisphere is uniform.

Consider the motion in *x*- and *y*-directions with coordinate (*x*,*y*) as indicated in the **Fig. 1**.

Horizontal motion – no acceleration

$$x = x(t) = (v_o \cos\theta)t \tag{1.1}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Vertical motion – ‘particle’ in free fall under gravity, $g$

$$y = y(t) = h + (v_o \sin\theta)t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 \tag{1.2}$$

**[0.3pt]**

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement:
Equation of water trajectory (or path of the projectile) is obtained by eliminating time $t$ from equations (1.1) and (1.2). **[0.1pt]**

Using Eq. (1.1), we get $t = \frac{x}{v_0 \cos\theta}$ and substituting $t$ in Eq.(1.2) we obtain **[0.1pt]**

$$y = h + x\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}\frac{1}{(\cos^2\theta)} \tag{1.3}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$= h + x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}(\sec^2\theta) \tag{1.4}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Using trigonometry identity: $\sec^2\theta = 1 + \tan^2\theta$, thus we write: **[0.1pt]**

$$y = h + x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta) \tag{1.5}$$

**[0.3pt]**

or

$$y' = y - h = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta) \tag{1.6}$$

The equation of water trajectory is given by Eq. (1.5) (with reference to the ground) or Eq. (1.6) with reference to the base of the hemisphere.

parts.label: A.3
parts.statement:
We rewrite the trajectory equation in the form of quadratic function in $\tan\theta$ **[0.2pt]**

$$\left(\frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}\right)\tan^2\theta - x\tan\theta + \left(y' + \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}\right) = 0 \tag{1.7}$$

**[0.5pt]**

where $y' = y - h$.

Let $\tan\theta = u$, thus we express Eq. (1.7) as a quadratic function in $u$:

$$au^2 + bu + c = 0 \tag{1.8}$$

**[0.3pt]**

where

$$a = \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}, \qquad b = -x, \qquad c = y' + \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}. \tag{1.9}$$

The quadratic equation Eq.(1.8) must have a real solution for $u$, i.e

$$u = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \tag{1.10}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Or the discriminant is non-negative, i.e. $b^2 - 4ac \geq 0$, which gives. **[0.2pt]**

$$x^2 - 4\left(\frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}\right)\left(y' + \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2}\right) \geq 0 \tag{1.11}$$

**[0.4pt]**

Re-arranging Eq.(1.11) for y’ to get

$$-y' \geq \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2} - \frac{v_o^2}{2g} \tag{1.12}$$

or

$$y' \leq \frac{v_o^2}{2g} - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2} \tag{1.13}$$

**[0.2pt]**

The water trajectory follows the inequality in (1.13) and the envelop of different water trajectories with different launch angles follow the parabolic equation:

$$y' = \frac{v_o^2}{2g} - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2} \tag{1.14}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Or

$$y = h + \frac{v_o^2}{2g} - \frac{gx^2}{2v_o^2} \tag{1.15}$$

**[0.3pt]**

The sketch of the envelop of water trajectory is shown below:

![Sketch of the envelop of water trajectory](p1-sol-fig1)

**[0.5pt]**

parts.label: A.4
parts.statement:
Recall the trajectory Eq. (1.5) and set $y = 0$ to obtain the horizontal range $x = R$:

$$0 = h + R\tan\theta - \frac{gR^2}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta) \tag{1.16}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$\frac{g}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)R^2 - (\tan\theta)R - h = 0 \tag{1.17}$$

**[0.2pt]**

which is a quadratic equation

$$a'R^2 + b'R + c' = 0 \tag{1.18}$$

**[0.2pt]**

with

$$a' = \frac{g}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta), \quad b' = -\tan\theta\,, \quad c = h., \tag{1.19}$$

The solution of Eq. (1.18) is the range of the water trajectory on the ground.

$$R = \frac{-b' \pm \sqrt{b'^2 - 4a'c'}}{2a'} \tag{1.20}$$

**[0.1pt]**

$$R = \frac{\tan\theta \pm \sqrt{\tan^2\theta + 4\frac{g}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)h}}{\frac{g}{v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)} \tag{1.21}$$

**[0.3pt]**

parts.label: A.5
parts.statement:
Letting $h = 0$ in Eq.(1.21) gives

$$R = \frac{\tan\theta \pm \sqrt{\tan^2\theta}}{\frac{g}{v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)} \tag{1.22}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$R = \frac{2\tan\theta}{\frac{g}{v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{\frac{g}{v_o^2}(\sec^2\theta)} \tag{1.23}$$

$$= \frac{v_o^2}{g}2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{v_o^2}{g}\sin 2\theta \tag{1.24}$$

**[0.3pt]**

sections.title: Part B: Non-Uniformly Distributed Holes on the Surface of the Hemisphere

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement:
Recall the range from (**A.4**) above (Eq. (1.21))

$$R = R(\theta) = \frac{\tan\theta \pm \sqrt{\tan^2\theta + 4\frac{g}{2v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)h}}{\frac{g}{v_o^2}(1 + \tan^2\theta)} \tag{1.21}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Let

$$\frac{dR}{d\theta} = R'(\theta) \tag{1.25}$$

**[0.2pt]**

and thus

$$dR = R'(\theta)d\theta. \tag{1.26}$$

**[0.2pt]**

There is no need to determine the R' explicitely. Answers can be left in R'. Consider an annulus (or ring) water on the ground with radius *R* and thickness *dR* where the element area of annulus $dA_W$ is given by

$$dA_W = 2\pi R \times dR \tag{1.27}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$= 2\pi RR'(\theta)d\theta \tag{1.28}$$

**[0.2pt]**

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement:
Number of holes in on the elemental area of annulus $dA_H$, on the hemisphere, of radius $r$ at angle $\theta$ with angular width $d\theta$ is

$$dA_H = \rho(\theta) \times 2\pi(r\ \cos\theta)rd\theta \tag{1.29}$$

**[0.2pt]**

In order the water sprouts to spray uniformly on the ground $dA_W \sim dA_H$ such that

$$dA_H = \rho(\theta) \times 2\pi(r\cos\theta)rd\theta \sim 2\pi RR'(\theta)d\theta \sim dA_W \tag{1.30}$$

**[0.4pt]**

And to ensure the expression is independent of $\rho(\theta)$, we express

$$\rho\left(\theta\right) \sim \frac{R(\theta)R'(\theta)}{r^2\cos\theta} \tag{1.31}$$

**[0.3pt]**

where $R(\theta)$ and $R'(\theta)$ are given by Eq. (1.21) and Eq.(1.25), respectively.

If the distribution of the holes on the hemisphere follows Eq. (1.31), then the water spray on the ground will be uniform (independent of angle). The condition set for angle $\theta$ does not affect the general expression in (1.31). **[0.1pt]**

parts.label: B.3
parts.statement:
When $h = 0$, the range become simple to estimate, namely from Eq. (1.24) we have

$$R(\theta) = \frac{v_o^2}{g}\sin 2\theta$$

**[0.2pt]**

and

$$\frac{dR(\theta)}{d\theta} = \frac{2v_o^2}{g}\cos 2\theta \tag{1.32}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$dR = \frac{2v_o^2}{g}\cos 2\theta\ d\theta \tag{1.33}$$

**[0.1pt]**

Consider an annulus (or ring) water on the ground with radius $R$ and thickness $dR$ where the element area of annulus $dA_W$ is given by

$$dA_W = 2\pi R \times dR$$

$$= 2\pi\left(\frac{v_o^2}{g}\sin 2\theta\right)\left(\frac{2v_o^2}{g}\cos 2\theta\right)d\theta \tag{1.34}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$= 2\pi\left(\frac{v_o^2}{g}\right)^2 2\sin 2\theta\cos 2\theta\ d\theta \tag{1.35}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$$= 2\pi\left(\frac{v_o^2}{g}\right)^2 \sin 4\theta\ d\theta \tag{1.36}$$

**[0.1pt]**

Thus, elemental area of water annulus $dA_W$ follows

$$dA_W \propto \sin 4\theta\ d\theta. \tag{1.37}$$

**[0.1pt]**

Recall from **B.2** the number of holes in on the elemental area of annulus $dA_H$, on the hemisphere, of radius $r$ at angle $\theta$ with angular width $d\theta$ is **[0.1pt]**

$$dA_H = \rho(\theta) \times 2\pi(r\ \cos(\theta))rd\theta \sim \rho(\theta)\cos(\theta)d\theta.$$

**[0.1pt]**

In order the water sprouts to spray uniformly on the ground $dA_W \propto dA_H$ such that **[0.1pt]**

$$dA_H \sim \rho(\theta)\cos\theta d\theta \sim \sin 4\theta\ d\theta. \tag{1.38}$$

**[0.3pt]**

And to ensure the expression is independent of $\rho(\theta)$, we express

$$\rho\left(\theta\right) \sim \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{\cos(\theta)}. \tag{1.39}$$

**[0.2pt]**

If the distribution of the holes per unit area on the hemisphere follows Eq. (1.39), then the water sprayed on the ground will be uniform (independent of angle). The condition set on the angle only to avoid duplication of water hitting the same area for $0^o < \theta \leq 45^o\ or\ 45^o < \theta < 90^o$. **[0.1pt]**

problems.title: Snell's Law
problems.statement:
**Introduction**

When light is incident upon a dielectric interface, it will be reflected and refracted, depending on the incident angle of the light and the refractive indices of the dielectric media as shown in **Fig. 1**. The refraction of light is governed by the Snell’s law,

$$n_1 \sin \phi_1 = n_2 \sin \phi_2 \tag{1}$$

where $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the refractive indices of the lower and upper parts of the boundary, $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ are the angles that the light ray makes with the normal of the boundary.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Refraction of light from a dielectric medium with refractive index, $n_1$, to a second dielectric medium with refractive index, $n_2$.
figures.alt: A horizontal boundary with a dashed vertical normal; a ray arrives from the lower medium n1 at angle ø1 to the normal and leaves into the upper medium at a larger angle ø2; the upper-left corner is labelled n2 < n1, the lower-left n1.

sections.title: Part A: Light Propagation Through a Semi-Sphere
sections.statement: **Fig. 2** illustrates how light that consists of two rays with different colour, $a$ and $b$, is incident along the radius of a semi-sphere with refractive index $n_x$, in air, before being refracted at the bottom at an angle of $\theta_a$ and $\theta_b$, respectively.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Light propagation through a semi-sphere.
figures.alt: A semi-sphere of refractive index nx with its flat face down; an incoming ray along a radius meets the centre of the flat face at angle θi to the dashed normal and splits below into two refracted rays a (angle θa) and b (angle θb, farther from the normal); the medium outside is labelled n2.

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement: Which ray ($a$ or $b$) propagates faster in the semi-sphere? Please provide justification.

answer.value: Ray a (colour a) propagates faster in the semi-sphere.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement: When the incident angle, $\theta_i$, is slowly increased to $45^{\mathrm{o}}$, ray $b$ no longer exits the bottom of the semi-sphere. When $\theta_i$ is further increased to $50^{\mathrm{o}}$, the same happens to ray $a$. What is the difference between the refractive index of ray $a$ and $b$ in the semi-sphere?

sections.title: Part B: Light Propagation Through a Cylindrical Rod
sections.statement: A cylindrical rod has a refractive index of $n_1$ = 1.50. The rod is placed in air, with one end coated with a polymer with refractive index $n_3$ = 1.40, as shown in **Fig. 3** below. Light is incident from the polymer into the rod at an angle, $\theta$. When $\theta$ is changed, there is an instance when light is totally reflected back to the polymer.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: A cylindrical rod with one end coated with a polymer with refractive index $n_3$, where $n_2 < n_3 < n_1$.
figures.alt: A long horizontal rod n1 (blue) in surrounding medium n2, its left end in a green polymer layer n3; a black ray enters from the polymer at angle θ to the dashed axis and zigzags along the rod by total internal reflection, and an orange ray is reflected back into the polymer.

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement: Determine the range of incident angle, $\theta$, for this condition to happen.

answer.note: В официалното решение ъгълът е отпечатан като „q“ (изгубен символ θ).

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement:
How does the condition in **B.1** change,

**(i)** if the other, open end of the rod is now coated with a thick layer of oil with refractive index of 1.60? **0.6pt**

**(ii)** if the setup is placed in water with refractive index of 1.33? **0.9pt**

answer.value: (i) Light cannot be totally reflected back to the polymer (condition #2 fails); (ii) conditions #1 and #2 do not overlap, so again light cannot be totally reflected back to the polymer.

sections.title: Part C: Light Propagation Through an Optical Fibre
sections.statement: Optical fibre is formed by surrounding the medium with refractive index, $n_1$ with a lower refractive index medium, $n_2$, as shown in **Fig. 4** below. The medium with refractive index, $n_1$ is known as the fibre core, and the medium with refractive index, $n_2$ is known as the fibre cladding. The refractive index, $n_3$, is typically the refractive index of air ($n_3$ = 1).

figures.caption: Fig. 4: A schematic of an optical fibre and its cross section.
figures.alt: Left: a 3D sketch of a cylindrical optical fibre with a dashed inner core. Right: a longitudinal cross section with core n1 between cladding layers n2 and outside medium n3; a ray enters the end face at angle θa to the dashed z axis and is reflected at the core–cladding boundary; axes r and z are marked.

parts.label: C.1
parts.statement: In order for light to propagate inside the optical fiber, it first needs to be coupled into the optical fiber. The maximum angle of the light incident at the end of the fiber, $\theta_a$ so that the light can be guided inside the fiber without being refracted out is related to the refractive indices of the fiber core and cladding. Consider a ray that propagates along the meridional plane (plane that cuts across the fibre axis), formulate the relationship between the angle, $\theta_a$ and the refractive indices.

parts.label: C.2
parts.statement: Optical fibers are not always aligned in a straight line but need to be bent to go through different spaces. Given the fiber core diameter of 50 $\mu\mathrm{m}$, if the minimum bending radius on the optical fiber is 1.0 $\mathrm{cm}$, how much will $\theta_a$ change?

parts.label: C.3
parts.statement: Given the refractive index of the fiber core and cladding is 1.45 and 1.44, respectively, what are the maximum angle of light incident for case **C.1** and **C.2** above, when the fiber is placed in air?

figures.caption: Rod with rays for conditions #1 and #2

figures.caption: Bent fibre: ray path through the straight and the bent section
figures.alt: A fibre with core n1 of width 50 μm between cladding layers n2 that bends downward on the right about a centre C far below; a ray enters at angle θa′, travels at θc and ϕc′ in the straight section, reaches point B on the lower boundary (angle ϕc′ to the normal) and point A on the upper boundary of the bent section (angle ϕc to the normal), where part of the light leaves the core; blue dotted lines join C to B and C to A.

sections.title: Part A: Light Propagation Through a Semi-Sphere

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement:
Using Snell’s law, larger angle of refraction corresponds to larger refractive index that the light sees in the semi-sphere ($n_1$). **[0.2pt]**

This means that the colour with a smaller angle of refraction propagates faster in the semi-sphere, which is colour *a*. **[0.3pt]**

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement:
The light rays no longer exit the bottom of semi-sphere when the ray is refracted by $90^{\mathrm{o}}$ with respect to the normal. **[0.2pt]**

Using Snell’s law,

$$n_x\sin\theta_i = n_2\sin(90^{\circ})$$

**[0.2pt]**

Replace “x” with “a” and “b” for the condition of ray a and ray b, respectively.

For ray a,

$$n_a\sin(50^{\circ}) = 1.0\sin(90^{\circ})$$

$$n_a = 1.305$$

**[0.2pt]**

For ray b,

$$n_b\sin(45^{\circ}) = 1.0\sin(90^{\circ})$$

$$n_b = 1.414$$

**[0.2pt]**

Difference in refractive index, Δn = **0.109** **[0.2pt]**

sections.title: Part B: Light Propagation Through a Cylindrical Rod

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement:
Given $n_1$ = 1.5, $n_2$ = 1.0, $n_3$ = 1.4,

![Rod with rays for conditions #1 and #2](p2-sol-fig1)

Identify 2 conditions that need to be obeyed: **[0.2pt]**

**#1: Light incident at point A should be totally reflected.**

$$n_1\sin\phi_1 > n_2\sin(90^{\circ})$$

$$\phi_1 > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.0}{1.5} = 41.81^{\circ}$$

**[0.3pt]**

The condition for angle $\theta_1 < 90^{\mathrm{o}} - 41.81^{\mathrm{o}} = 48.19^{\mathrm{o}}$ **[0.2pt]**

Using Snell’s law,

$$\theta < \sin^{-1}\frac{1.5}{1.4}\sin(48.19^{\circ}) = 53^{\circ}$$

**[0.2pt]**

**#2: Light incident at point B should be totally reflected.**

$$n_1\sin\theta_2 > n_2\sin(90^{\circ})$$

$$\theta_2 > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.0}{1.5} = 41.81^{\circ}$$

**[0.3pt]**

The condition for angle $q_1 > 41.81^{\mathrm{o}}$ **[0.2pt]**

Using Snell's Law

$$\theta > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.5}{1.4}\sin(41.81^{\circ}) = 45.58^{\circ}$$

**[0.2pt]**

Therefore, the incident angle, $q$, where light is totally reflected back to the polymer is $45.58^{\mathrm{o}} < q < 53^{\mathrm{o}}$. **[0.4pt]**

parts.label: B.2 (i)
parts.statement:
When right end of rod is coated with oil with $n_4$ = 1.6, condition #2 changes. **[0.2pt]**

Light incident on point B will always be refracted. **[0.2pt]**

Light CANNOT be totally reflected back to the polymer. **[0.2pt]**

parts.label: B.2 (ii)
parts.statement:
When the setup is placed in water, **$n_2$ = 1.33**. Both condition #1 and #2 change. **[0.2pt]**

#1:

$$\phi_1 > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.33}{1.5} = 62.46^{\circ}$$

**[0.2pt]**

$\theta_1 < 90^{\mathrm{o}} - 62.46^{\mathrm{o}} = 27.54^{\mathrm{o}}$

Using Snell’s law,

$$\theta < \sin^{-1}\frac{1.5}{1.4}\sin(27.54^{\circ}) = 29.7^{\circ}$$

#2:

$$\theta_2 > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.33}{1.5} = 62.46^{\circ}$$

Using Snell’s law,

$$\theta > \sin^{-1}\frac{1.5}{1.4}\sin(62.46^{\circ}) = 71.81^{\circ}$$

**[0.2pt]**

As conditions #1 and #2 does not overlap. **[0.1pt]**

Again, light CANNOT be totally reflected back to the polymer. **[0.2pt]**

sections.title: Part C: Light Propagation Through an Optical Fibre

parts.label: C.1
parts.statement:
![Ray entering the fibre core and meeting the core/cladding boundary at the critical angle](p2-sol-fig2)

In order for light to not refractive out from the fiber, the angle of refraction that the light makes with the normal of the fiber core/cladding boundary needs to be $90^{\mathrm{o}}$. Using Snell’s law,

$$n_1\sin\phi_c = n_2\sin(90^{\circ}) \tag{1}$$

**[0.4pt]**

Taking the square of eq. (1), we have,

$$n_1^2\sin^2\phi_c = n_2^2$$

Using the trigonometry identity, we have, **[0.2pt]**

$$n_1^2(1 - \cos^2\phi_c) = n_2^2$$

Rearranging, we got,

$$n_1^2\cos^2\phi_c = n_1^2 - n_2^2$$

Or, **[0.2pt]**

$$n_1^2\sin^2\theta_c = n_1^2 - n_2^2 \tag{2}$$

Taking the square root of eq. (2), we have,

$$n_1\sin\theta_c = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$

**[0.4pt]**

With this, we can use Snell’s law to calculate the maximum angle of light incident,

$$n_3\sin\theta_a = n_1\sin\theta_c = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$

**[0.4pt]**

$$\theta_a = \sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}}{n_3}$$

**[0.4pt]**

or $\theta_a = \sin^{-1}\sqrt{{n_1}^2 - {n_2}^2}$

parts.label: C.2
parts.statement:
![Bent fibre: ray path through the straight and the bent section](p2-sol-fig3)

- Identifying the correct relationship between $\phi_c$and $\phi'_c$ **[0.4pt]**

- Find the relationship between $\phi_c$ and $\phi_c$’:

- Using the Law of Sine,

$$\sin\phi_c = \frac{CB}{CA}\sin(\pi - \phi_c')$$

**[0.4pt]**

- For light guiding at point A,

$$\sin\phi_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

**[0.4pt]**

CB = 10000-25 = 9975 $\mu$m

CA = 10000+25 = 10025 $\mu$m **[0.4pt]**

$$\sin(\pi - \phi_c') = \sin(\phi_c')$$

Therefore,

$$\sin(\phi_c') = \frac{10025n_2}{9975n_1}$$

**[0.4pt]**

Rearrange into eq.(1) and derive following part (a):

$$a.n_1\sin(\phi_c') = n_2, \qquad where\ a = \frac{9975}{10025}$$

$$a^2\,n_1^2\sin^2(\phi_c') = n_2^2$$

$$a^2n_1^2(1 - \cos^2\phi'_c) = n_2^2$$

$$a^2n_1^2\cos^2\phi'_c = a^2n_1^2 - n_2^2$$

$$a^2n_1^2\sin^2\theta'_c = a^2n_1^2 - n_2^2$$

$$n_1\sin\theta'_c = \frac{1}{a}\sqrt{a^2n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$

**[0.4pt]**

To calculate the new angle of acceptance,

$$n_3\sin\theta'_a = n_1\sin\theta'_c = \frac{1}{a}\sqrt{a^2n_1^2 - n_2^2}$$

$$\theta'_a = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{10025}{9975n_3}\sqrt{a^2n_1^2 - n_2^2}\right)$$

**[0.2pt]**

problems.title: The First Discovered Quasar: Unveiling the Mysteries of the Astrophysical Source 3C 273

sections.title: Part A: Moon's Apparent Motion Against the Background Stars
sections.statement: The Moon takes 27.3 days to complete 1 orbit of the Earth with respect to the stars, a period known as a sidereal month. Through a telescope, the moon’s motion is readily apparent, but to the eye, it requires careful observation over several hours to notice the Moon’s changing position. Remembering that 3600 arcseconds = 60 arcminutes = 1 degree then, through how many degrees, arcminutes, and arcseconds does the Moon move against the background of stars in

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement: one hour? One minute? One second?

answer.value: ≈ 0.55° (33 arcminutes, ≈ 1978 arcseconds) per hour; ≈ 0.0092° (0.55 arcminutes, 33 arcseconds) per minute; ≈ 0.000153° (0.0092 arcminutes, ≈ 0.55 arcseconds) per second.
answer.note: В официалното решение последният ред е отпечатан като „0.55deg per second of time“ — по смисъла на пресмятането това са дъгови секунди; текстът на решението е запазен както е отпечатан.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement: How long does it take the Moon to move a distance equal to its own diameter on the sky? (Note: the angular diameter of the moon as viewed from Earth is 30 arcminutes)

sections.title: Part B: Using Lunar Occultations to Precisely Determine Radio Source Positions: The Case of 3C 273
sections.statement:
In the late 1950s and early 1960s, radio position measurements with this precision were not available. While occultations had been used previously, Hazard was specifically interested in their ability to determine radio positions and structure with arcsecond precision. Such measurements were made in the optical reference frame thereby allowing reliable optical identifications. Hazard had noted that the strong Class II radio source 3C 273 would be hidden by the Moon (also known as occultation) several times during 1962 and 1963.

The 1962 August 5 occultation was undertaken at 410 and 136 MHz. Both disappearance and reappearance were observed and the disappearance record revealed the presence of two components, A and B, in the source. The disappearance on the right and the reappearance records on the left, at 410 MHz are plotted in **Fig. 1**.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The 1962 August 5 disappearance and reappearance records at 410 MHz, taken from Hazard et al. (1963). Note that time increases from right to left, and that the Moon is also moving from right to left. The bottom panel shows the positions of source components A and B relative to the limb of the Moon at disappearance and reappearance.
figures.alt: Two chart-recorder traces of radio intensity on a grid, with an arrow 'Time' pointing left and a '1 minute' scale bar: the left panel (reappearance) shows oscillations and a peak before a drop to the baseline, the right panel (disappearance) shows a rise with two steps marked A and B by arrows. Below, a dark band labelled 'Moon’s motion' with a leftward arrow and 'LIMB OF MOON' on both sides, with dots for components A and B at each limb.

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement:
What is causing the oscillation in the observed intensity?

A. The diffraction pattern of the telescope

B. Instabilities in the mount of the telescope

C. The features of the surface of the Moon

D. Earth's atmospheric conditions

answer.note: A. The diffraction pattern of the telescope.

parts.label: B.2
parts.statement:
Why there is no extra bump for the B component in the left plot for the reappearance of the source? How does it help to understand the structure of the source?

A. The two components have been orbiting around the Moon.

B. Our line-of-sight has changed with respect to the two components.

C. Both components are aligned with the limb of the Moon when they reappear.

D. The time scales of the physics behind the luminosity of the two components were long enough to make one of them fade.

answer.note: C. Both components are aligned with the limb of the Moon when they reappear.

parts.label: B.3
parts.statement: Based on your answer in **A.1** to **A.4**, and the data in **Fig. 1**, estimate the approximate apparent (projected) angular separation between the two components of 3C 273.

answer.note: Официалното решение приема всяка обоснована оценка от този порядък.

sections.title: Part C: The Breakthrough Discovery of 3C 273's True Nature
sections.statement: In 1962, the year of these observations, Maarten Schmidt was working on the programme of optical identification and spectroscopy of the optical objects identified with radio sources. Whiteoak mentions as an afterthought that the ‘current Caltech thinking’ is that the potential 3C 273 identification is with a star and a strange jet. Given that no other bright star had been proposed as a radio source identification, he assumed that the bright magnitude 13 ‘star’ (magnitude accounts as a way to measure how bright a star is; the brighter the star, the smaller the number) was merely a confusing foreground very bright star. To obtain a spectrum of the faint jet, which he saw as by far the most likely identification, it was inevitable that the bright confusing star some arcseconds away would spill over into any spectrum of the jet he would obtain. To offset this, Maarten Schmidt had decided to first obtain a spectrum of this bright star. On the night of December 29, he managed to obtain a spectrum of the bright ‘star’ which showed some faint emission lines (**Fig. 2**), but with no obvious explanation in terms of any expected stellar lines. Only when Schmidt decided to compare the strange spectrum with the Balmer lines of hydrogen, things became clear:

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Optical spectrum of 3C 273 (top) together with a comparison laboratory spectrum (bottom).
figures.alt: Two spectra from Red (left) to Blue (right): the upper one labelled 3C 273 with lines Hβ, Hγ, Hδ bracketed above it and an arrow 'Red shift' pointing left from a dashed vertical line; the lower comparison spectrum with Hβ, Hγ, Hδ bracketed below and arrows marking 600 nm, 500 nm and 400 nm; label 'Comparison spectrum'; small print 'Copyright © 2008 Pearson Education, Inc., publishing as Pearson Addison-Wesley.'

parts.label: C.1
parts.statement: Compare the wavelength ratios of the lines shown in **Fig. 2**. Based on these ratios, what is the redshift $z = \frac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}$ of this source?

answer.note: Оценка по фигурата; официалното решение приема близки стойности при разумно оценени дължини на вълната.

parts.label: C.2
parts.statement: Consider that this redshift is arising due to relativistic gravitational effects from the mass of the object. In this case, we can estimate the gravitational redshift as $z = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \frac{2GM}{c^2 r}}} - 1$. Prove that, whether you put 3C 273 at any distance (e.g, edge of the Milky Way, $r \sim$ 100 kpc $\sim 3 \times 10^{21}$ m; edge of the Solar System, $r \sim$ 100 AU $\sim 1.5 \times 10^{13}$ m), the mass of 3C 273 would be so large it would disrupt the entire galaxy / solar system.

answer.value: M ∼ 10^17 M⊙ at 100 kpc (more than the mass of the Milky Way); M ∼ 10^9 M⊙ at 100 au (would disrupt the Solar System).

parts.label: C.3
parts.statement: Hubble's law states that the farther the galaxies, the faster they are moving away from Earth. The Hubble's constant is the ratio between the speed and the distance of those galaxies, and equal to H=75 km/s/Mpc. With this idea in mind, we can consider instead that the calculated redshift is due to the cosmological expansion, and we can approximate that $z \sim v/c$. In that case, what is the distance of this object? Compare this with the size of the Milky Way.

answer.note: Хиляди пъти по-далеч от размера на Млечния път.

sections.title: Part D: The Intrinsic Luminosity of the Radio Source 3C 273
sections.statement:
The flux of the source 3C 273 has been measure across the radio spectrum and has been found to follow the equation $F_
u \sim 25000
u^{(-0.3)}\ \mathrm{Jy}$, where $
u$ is the observed frequency in Hertz and a Jansky is defined as $1\ \mathrm{Jy} = 10^{-26}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,Hz^{-1}}$. Of course, since the source is radiating over a sphere of radius the distance from us, the intrinsic luminosity will be given by $L_
u = 4\pi d^2 F_
u$. With this,

parts.label: D.1
parts.statement:
What is the luminosity of the source per unit frequency?

(help: $1\ \mathrm{pc} = 3.09 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{m}$)

answer.note: В официалното решение единицата е отпечатана като „W m^-2 Hz^-1“ (за светимост на единица честота е W Hz^-1); оставена е както е отпечатана.

parts.label: D.2
parts.statement: What is the total luminosity in the radio band (ie., from $10^7$ Hz to $10^{11}$ Hz)?

parts.label: D.3
parts.statement: How does the luminosity of 3C 273 compare with the luminosity of the Sun ( $L_{sun} = 3.82 \times 10^{26}$ W) and the Milky Way ($L_{MW} = 1.5 \times 10^{10} L_{sun}$) in the same frequency range?

answer.note: L/L_sun ≈ 2.3 × 10^11; по-ярък и от Млечния път.

sections.title: Part E: The Power Source of 3C 273
sections.statement: We have seen that the brightness of 3C 273 is too large for a single star, even for an entire galaxy. Therefore, there should be another mechanism, other than stars, producing all this power.

parts.label: E.1
parts.statement: Check that the annihilation of matter with antimatter (e.g., $\mathrm{e}^+ + \mathrm{e}^- \to 2\gamma$) would not explain this, since it would produce very energetic X-rays rays rather than optical and radio emission.

answer.value: The annihilation photons (0.5 MeV each) have wavelength ≈ 0.000002 nm — well within the X-rays, not optical or radio.
answer.note: В официалното решение енергията е отпечатана като „8 × 10^14 J“ (положителен показател); оставена е както е отпечатана.

parts.label: E.2
parts.statement: Something that was immediately proposed was the accretion of matter into a supermassive black hole. Let’s check that potential energy can give all this energy: Consider that the black hole accretes one solar mass ($2 \times 10^{30}$ kg) towards its Schwarzschild radius ($R_s = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$) every year. What is the power that can be obtained for the accretion? Would this be enough to explain the observations discussed in D1 to D3?

answer.note: ≈ 1.8 × 10^47 J/yr; с порядък повече от необходимото, така че е достатъчно.

sections.title: Part F: Modern Observations and the Nature of 3C 273's Components
sections.statement:
Modern images from various telescopes (see e.g., **Fig. 3**) have found that the two components A and B that were measured with the lunar occultation actually refer to a compact core, which hosts the black hole, and a jet that extends the distance that you calculated before. This jet is thought to be produced via acceleration of the accreted particles via the strong black hole magnetic field, in a similar way particles from the Solar wind hit the magnetic field of Earth to produce the auroras near the poles, but at much larger scale.

The energy density required for the production of such jet can be written in terms of the magnetic fields as the sum of the particle energy density $U_e \sim B^{(-3/2)}$ and the magnetic energy density $U_B \sim B^2$.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Radio image of 3C 273 taken with the MERLIN telescope.
figures.alt: False-colour radio image on a dark blue background: a bright compact dot in the upper left (the core) and a faint blue jet extending diagonally to the lower right, ending in a bright red-yellow knot.

parts.label: F.1
parts.statement: Show that the minimum energy density is given by $\frac{U_e}{U_B} = \frac{4}{3}$

parts.label: F.2
parts.statement:
If we assume that the total power of the 3C 273 jet is given by half of the energy released by 3C 273 in one second calculated in D.1 and D.2, and the jet has a volume of $10^{45}\ \mathrm{m^3}$, estimate the magnetic field of the jet.

(hint: use that the magnetic permeability is $4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$)

sections.title: Part A: Moon's Apparent Motion Against the Background Stars

parts.label: A.1
parts.statement:
The moon completes one orbit in about a month, or more quantitatively, moves through **360 degrees in 27.3 days**. 360 divided by 27.3 = 13.19 degrees per day. Each day the moon will appear about **13deg** to the **east** of its position at the same time on the previous day.

Now convert to motion per hour. 13.19 degrees/day divided by 24 hrs/day = 0.55 degrees/hr. The moon passes through a little more than ½ of a degree in one hour of time. **[0.5pt]**

Since 1deg = 60 arcminutes, then 0.55deg = 33 arcminutes (this is a ratio, 1:60 as 0.55:33). Therefore the moon moves through 33 arcminutes per hour of time.

Since 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds, then the moon moves through 33 x 60 arcseconds in a hour = 1978 arcsec per hour of time.

Moving 0.55 degrees / hr divided by 60 minutes per hr = 0.0092 degrees / min. The moon moves through a small fraction of a degree in one minute of time.

As 1deg = 60 arcminutes, then 0.0092deg = 0.55 arcminutes. The moon moves through 0.55 arcminutes per minute of time. **[0.4pt]**

Since 1 arcminute = 60 arcseconds, the moon moves through 33 arcseconds per minute of time.

Moving 0.55 degrees per hour divided by 3600 seconds per hour = 0.000153 degrees in a second of time.

If the moon moves 0.55 arcminute per minute of time (from part b) then the moon will move 0.55 / 60 = 0.0092 arcminutes in one second of time. **[0.4pt]**

0.0092 arcminutes X 60 arcseconds per arcminute = 0.55deg per second of time.

parts.label: A.2
parts.statement:
The diameter of the moon = 30 arcminutes = 0.5 degree (given in the notes).

From part (b), the moon moves through 0.55 arcminutes per minute of time

The time it takes to move a specific distance = that distance divided by the rate of motion. The time it take the Moon to move one lunar diameter = distance traveled (30 arcminutes) / divided by rate (0.55 arcminutes per minute) = 54.5 minutes, just under an hour. **[0.5pt]**

sections.title: Part B: Using Lunar Occultations to Precisely Determine Radio Source Positions: The Case of 3C 273

parts.label: B.1
parts.statement: The correct answer is: A. The diffraction pattern of the telescope. **[0.6pt]**

parts.label: B.2

The student can check the figure to estimate the wavelengths by eye where certain emission lines are happening. The reasoning shall be written. The resulting redshift of 3C273 is $(\lambda-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0 \sim 0.158$. Other results that are similar to this one will be also considered correct as long as the wavelengths are reasonably estimated. **[0.3pt]**

Solving for the mass, we have that $M=(c^2r/2G)[1-1/(1+z)^2]$. **[0.2pt]**

If we put it at the edge of the Milky Way (at 100 kpc), then $r \sim 3 \times 10^{21}$ m and $M \sim 10^{17} M_\odot$ (larger than the entire mass of the Milky Way!) **[0.2pt]**

if we put it at the edge of the Solar System (at 100 au), then $r \sim 1.5 \times 10^{13}$ m and $M \sim 10^{9} M_\odot$. This would totally disrupt the Solar System. **[0.2pt]**

parts.label: C.3
parts.statement:
Since $z \sim v/c$ for small redshift and Hubble’s law is $v = Hd$, we can combine these two equations to obtain $d = zc/H$. **[0.3pt]**

If we use that H=75 km/s/Mpc, then $d = 0.158*300\ 000 / 75 \sim 632$ Mpc. (The current estimation is that the distance is 749 Mpc). This is thousands of times farther away than the size of the Milky Way, and must therefore, be an independent object very much farther away. **[0.3pt]**

parts.label: E.1
parts.statement:
We are going to be using the mass-energy expression. Electrons have a mass-energy of 0.5 MeV (other units; e.g, $8 \times 10^{14}$J will also be considered valid). **[0.4pt]**

parts.label: E.2
parts.statement: The gravitational potential energy of a mass m is given by $W=-GMm/r$. Since the smallest radius the particle reaches is the Schwarzschild radius, $W = -GMmc^2/2GM = -mc^2/2$. This is still an order of magnitude more than what is needed to power 3C273, so it even leaves room for a certain efficiency. **[0.7pt]**

**[0.2pt]**

Doing each of the terms separately,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}U_e}{\mathrm{d}B} = -\frac{3}{2}B^{-5/2} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{U_e}{B}$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}U_b}{\mathrm{d}B} = 2B = \frac{2U_b}{B}$$

Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}B} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{U_e}{B} + \frac{2U_b}{B} = 0 \to \frac{U_e}{U_b} = \frac{4}{3}$ **[0.5pt]**

parts.label: F.2
parts.statement:
The total energy, from the calculations in terms of the magnetic energy is $U = \frac{7}{3}U_b$.

Therefore, If $U = \frac{1}{2} \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{J}$, then the magnetic energy will be $U_b = \frac{3}{14} \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{J}$. **[0.3pt]**

For a volume of $10^{45}\ \mathrm{m}^3$, the energy density will be $u_b = \frac{\frac{3}{14}\times10^{38}\ \mathrm{J}}{10^{45}\ \mathrm{m}^3} = 0.21 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{J/m}^3$. **[0.2pt]**

Now, since $u = \frac{B^2}{2\mu}$, with $\mu$ = magnetic permeability = $4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{Tm/A}$, we have that $B = \sqrt{2 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 0.21 \times 10^{-7}} \sim 2.3 \times 10^{-7}$ Tesla. **[0.2pt]**
